# Extensive-form game catalogue {#sec-extensive-form-catalogue .unnumbered}

```{=typst}
// This unnumbered catalogue uses local figure numbers.
#show figure.where(kind: "quarto-float-fig"): set figure(numbering: "1")
```

Circles denote player decisions, diamonds labelled $c$ denote chance, and dashed
links join nodes in one information set. Unless stated otherwise,
terminal pairs are ordered $(\text{player 1},\text{player 2})$.
The examples below are used in
[Lecture 7](../lectures/07-extensive-form-games.qmd#sec-efg-perfect-information).

## Alice–Bob game

The game tree from [Strategic games](../lectures/01-strategic-games.qmd#the-alicebob-game).

```{mermaid}
%%| file: extensive-form/contingent-plans.mmd
%%| label: fig-catalogue-alice-bob
%%| fig-cap: "Alice and Bob plan an evening. Payoffs are preference scores ordered (Alice, Bob)."
%%| fig-alt: "Alice first chooses to stay home, action a, or go out, action b. After staying home, Bob chooses an action film, c, or cooking together, d. After going out, Bob chooses a cafe, e, or live music, f; following live music, Alice chooses a rock club, g, or a jazz club, h. The five terminal payoffs are 0 comma 4; 2 comma 1; 1 comma 2; 3 comma 8; and 8 comma 0."
%%| fig-width: 8
```

## A game with chance moves {#sec-catalogue-chance-moves}

{{< var games.chance_moves.rules >}}

![A game with chance moves. Players are labelled 1 and 2; chance is labelled $c$. Terminal pairs give utilities in the order (player 1, player 2).](../games/extensive-form/chance-moves.svg){#fig-catalogue-chance-moves width=90% fig-alt="Player 1 chooses a or b. After a, player 2 chooses c for (1, 3) or d for (4, 1). After b, chance gives (2, 2) with probability one half or a further player 1 decision with probability one half. Player 1 chooses e or f. Action f gives (3, 3); e leads to (0, 4), (4, 2), (8, 0) with probabilities one quarter, one half, one quarter."}

See @sec-efg-chance for expected-utility calculations and backward induction.
The subgame-perfect equilibrium is $((b,e),c)$, with expected payoffs $(3,2)$.

## A basic poker endgame {#sec-catalogue-poker-endgame}

{{< var games.poker_endgame.rules >}}

![A basic poker endgame. Player 1 sees the card; player 2 observes the bet but cannot distinguish the two nodes in the dashed information set.](../games/extensive-form/poker-endgame.svg){#fig-catalogue-poker-endgame width=100% fig-alt="Chance deals W with probability one quarter or L with probability three quarters. Player 1 checks or bets at separate nodes. Checks pay (1, -1) for W and (-1, 1) for L. After a bet, player 2's nodes are linked: folding pays (1, -1), while calling pays (3, -3) for W and (-3, 3) for L."}

## Kuhn poker {#sec-catalogue-kuhn-poker}

{{< var games.kuhn_poker.rules >}}

For a deal $(x,y)$, $x$ is player 1's private card and $y$ is player
2's. The diagrams separate dealing from betting; the full game
contains one betting continuation for each of the six deals.

![The dealing stage of Kuhn poker. Each ordered deal has probability 1/6. Dashed links join player 1's opening nodes with the same private card; betting continues below every node.](../games/extensive-form/kuhn-poker-deal.svg){#fig-catalogue-kuhn-poker-deal width=100% fig-alt="Chance selects one of (J,Q), (J,K), (Q,J), (Q,K), (K,J), (K,Q), each with probability one sixth. Player 1's six opening nodes are grouped into three information sets according to the first card."}

![The betting continuation for one fixed deal (x,y). Here w is 1 if x is higher than y and -1 otherwise. Information sets connecting different deals are omitted from this slice.](../games/extensive-form/kuhn-poker-betting.svg){#fig-catalogue-kuhn-poker-betting width=100% fig-alt="Player 1 checks or bets. After a check, player 2 checks for payoff (w, -w), or bets; player 1 then folds for (-1, 1) or calls for (2w, -2w). After an opening bet, player 2 folds for (1, -1) or calls for (2w, -2w)."}

Each player's information sets are determined by their own card
and the public betting history. There are six information sets per
player. In particular, different deals must be linked when these
observations agree:

![One information set in Kuhn poker: player 2 holds Q and faces an opening bet. The opponent may hold J or K, but the response must use the same distribution at both nodes.](../games/extensive-form/kuhn-poker-information.svg){#fig-catalogue-kuhn-poker-information width=90% fig-alt="A partial tree shows histories (J,Q,bet) and (K,Q,bet) joined in player 2's information set. A fold gives (1, -1) at either node. A call gives (-2, 2) against J and (2, -2) against K."}

See @sec-efg-kuhn-poker for the complete list of information sets
and terminal betting sequences [@schmid2025efg].

## Forgetting an earlier decision {#sec-catalogue-forgotten-visit}

{{< var games.forgotten_visit.rules >}}

![An imperfect-recall decision problem. The dashed link joins two visits to the same information set, one before and one after the player's own action A.](../games/extensive-form/forgotten-visit.svg){#fig-catalogue-forgotten-visit width=85% fig-alt="One player acts at two nodes in the same information set. B at the root gives 0, while A continues. At the second node A gives 1 and B gives 4. The player forgets the earlier visit and action."}

There is only one player, so each terminal label is a single payoff.
This example permits repeated visits to an information set and
violates perfect recall. See @sec-efg-perfect-recall for the
different outcomes of mixed plans and fresh randomization at each visit.
